35 The charge that a fully charged 12 V car battery can supply is 100 kC. The starter motor of the car
requires a current of 200 A for an average period of 2.0 s. The battery does not recharge because
of a fault.
What is the maximum number of times the starter motor of the car can be used?
A
21
B
25
C
42
D
250

hints: Notice the two charge quantities: total stored charge is $100 \text{ kC} = 100000 \text{ C}$, while each start draws $200 \text{ A}$ for $2.0 \text{ s}$.
Recall current as rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$, so the charge for one use is $Q = It$ with $I$ in amperes and $t$ in seconds.
Calculate $Q$ for one $2.0 \text{ s}$ start first, then divide the total $100000 \text{ C}$ by that value to find how many whole starts are possible.
walkthrough: Identify the total charge available: $Q_{total} = 100 \text{ kC} = 100 \times 1000 \text{ C} = 100000 \text{ C}$. The $12 \text{ V}$ is not needed for a charge calculation.
State the governing relation for current: $I = Q/t$, rearranged to charge delivered in time $t$ as $Q = It$.
Substitute the starter motor values with units: $Q_{one} = 200 \text{ A} \times 2.0 \text{ s} = 400 \text{ C}$ for one average use.
Find the maximum number $N$ of uses by dividing total charge by charge per use: $N = Q_{total}/Q_{one} = 100000/400$.
Calculate and check units: $N = 250$, a dimensionless count, with charge in coulombs cancelling. This is option D.

A.explanation: 21 uses only about $8400 \text{ C}$ in total, far less than the $100 \text{ kC}$ available, so it greatly underestimates the number of starts.

B.explanation: 25 is obtained if $100 \text{ kC}$ is taken as $100 \text{ C}$, giving $100/400$, so it forgets the kilo prefix $1 \text{ kC} = 1000 \text{ C}$.

C.explanation: 42 would need about $2380 \text{ C}$ per $2.0 \text{ s}$ start, about six times the correct $400 \text{ C}$, so it overestimates charge per use.

D.explanation: One start uses $Q = It = 400 \text{ C}$ and $100000 \text{ C} / 400 \text{ C} = 250$ uses, matching the total charge available.
